newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Rebel gains bring peace no closer to Afghanistan.
newsitem.headline: Rebel gains bring peace no closer to Afghanistan.

text.p: The rebel Taleban militia is unlikely to topple the Kabul government despite its dramatic recent gains in eastern Afghanistan, diplomats said on Monday.

They said the Taleban advances were a setback to the government but would not shift the balance of power decisively or end the civil war which has ripped the impoverished country apart since the fall of a communist government in April 1992.
The latest fighting also clouds prospects for U.N. efforts to broker a peace settlement between warring factions.
The Taleban, a militant Sunni Moslem movement started by Afghan students at religious schools in Pakistan two years ago, captured the eastern city of Jalalabad on Wednesday.
The victory, achieved with little fighting, forced neutral faction leader Haji Abdul Qadir to flee to Pakistan and made the Taleban masters of the vital Jalalabad-Pakistan road link.

The Taleban now hold most of the areas previously controlled by the Hezb-i-Islami party of Gulbuddin Hekmatyar, who rejoined the Kabul government as prime minister in May under a peace pact with his old enemy President Burhanuddin Rabbani.
The Islamic warriors are now consolidating their grip on nearby provinces before a possible attack on the government-held town of Sarobi, about 70 km (37 miles) east of Kabul.

Forces loyal to Rabbani, who hold only five of Afghanistan's 33 provinces, are digging into new defences around Sarobi, which straddles the Jalalabad-Kabul road and controls access to the Tagab Valley leading to the government's main airbase at Bagram.
"If there is going to be a major military confrontation, I would expect it to be at Sarobi," said a Western military analyst. "The fate of Kabul could rest on that battle."
But a Pakistani foreign ministry source said Rabbani's top commander Ahmad Shah Masood could still hold off an assault on the Afghan capital even if the Taleban took Sarobi.

"Sarobi is less strategic than before because the Taleban already control Jalalabad and the road from Pakistan," he said. "The Taleban may be able to take it as it is an ethnic Pashtun area, but Masood will be able to defend Tajik areas."
The Taleban draw most of their support from Afghanistan's traditionally dominant Pashtun community. The Kabul government is dominated by Tajiks, including Rabbani and Masood.
Northern rebel General Abdul Rashid Dostum, an Uzbek, leads a third main ethnic group, while two Shi'ite Moslem factions vie for the loyalty of the Hazaras of central Afghanistan.
Shi'ite Iran, deeply hostile to the Taleban, is pressing Dostum to ally with the government against the Sunni militants.

Dostum, the next logical target for the Taleban if they defeat Masood's forces, threw a lifeline to the government last month by opening the Salang highway linking Kabul to the north, but diplomats say he is reluctant to commit himself further.
"He is still keeping his options open," the foreign ministry source said. "He wants to maintain his independent position."
The source said Iran was training and arming 20,000 Afghans under the command of former Herat provincial governor Ismail Khan, driven out of the western city by the Taleban a year ago.
"We think this will worsen the situation," he said.
Iran, like Pakistan, denies backing any Afghan faction. Rabbani and Masood have often accused Islamabad of supporting the Taleban to promote its own interests in Afghanistan.
The Taleban, vowing to oust Rabbani and install a purist Islamic order throughout the country, have refused talks with the government until the president steps down.
They also abhor the idea of openly collaborating with Dostum, whom they regard as tainted by his communist past.

U.N. under-secretary for political affairs Marrack Goulding, who has been visiting Afghan leaders in a bid to hammer out a peace formula, said last week it was "common knowledge" that several regional countries were involved in the Afghan conflict.
He also said that the Taleban had not shown they had given up the military option.
"Only Dostum seems ready to accept any settlement," said the Pakistani foreign ministry source. "We are encouraging all factions to talk but Masood and the Taleban aren't interested."
